steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for our paper proposing a knowledge distillation method for LLMs based on the Sinkhorn distance. Cover why existing logits-based divergence measures fall short, the problem with sample-wise KD, our method and its batch-wise reformulation, how we evaluate it, and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs, their size, and the need for knowledge distillation
2. Logits-based KD and the limits of KL / RKL / JS divergences
3. Limits of sample-wise KD on LLMs
4. SinKD: Sinkhorn distance as divergence measure
5. Batch-wise reformulation
6. Experiments: comparability, validity, generalizability
7. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs and KD
- BERT, RoBERTa, T0, GPT: SOTA records on many NLP tasks
- scaling laws -> models with billions of parameters
- model size makes deployment under resource-constrained environments unaffordable
- KD: cost-efficient approach, distill smaller models with highly competitive performance

2. Logits-based KD and divergence measures
- measure and minimize divergence between teacher and student logit distributions; key = proper measurement
- existing: KL, RKL, JS divergences
- all variants of f-divergence; limited for distributions lacking substantial intersections
- Fig. 1: each has own drawbacks
- KL: mode-averaging, student learns overly smooth distribution covering whole teacher support
- RKL: mode-collapsing, student focuses on one highly probable region, ignores the rest
- JS: mode-underestimation, underestimates rare events due to insufficient penalty

3. Sample-wise KD on LLMs
- discriminative tasks: low-dimensional categorical outputs give limited insight into high-dimensional hidden distributions
- intuitive fix: use a batch of samples to collectively grasp distribution differences
- existing divergences handle each sample independently (logit-by-logit); not distance metrics, cannot locate paired teacher/student logits of same sample in a batch

4. SinKD
- Sinkhorn Knowledge Distillation (SinKD); logits-based KD for generalizability
- Sinkhorn distance = variant of Wasserstein distance
- Wasserstein: minimum cost to transform one distribution into the other; more sensible cost function; differentiable almost everywhere
- but hard to compute analytically; cost prohibitively high for LLMs
- Sinkhorn: efficient approximation, keeps the benefits, mitigates cost

5. Batch-wise reformulation
- sample-wise use feasible but does not exploit perception of structural differences
- Sinkhorn: symmetric metric; derived from optimal transport (OT) -> explicit constraints on matching correctness
- teacher/student batch outputs as sets A and B; minimizing overall distance enforces element-wise matching of same-sample outputs
- -> batch-wise reformulation; capture geometric structures of implicit distributions via low-dimensional observations
- no extra network layer, no task-specific output format changes

6. Experiments
- comparability: BERT on GLUE, consistently beats SOTA KD methods
- validity: ablations and hyper-parameters; advice for practitioners
- generalizability: SuperGLUE with various architectures, encoder-decoder T0 to decoder-only GPT-Neo; prior work only encoder-only BERT

7. Contributions
- SinKD with Sinkhorn distance: addresses KL/RKL/JS limits in extreme scenarios, avoids Wasserstein computation burden
- properties of Sinkhorn distance -> batch-wise OT reformulation
- experiments show superiority over SOTA; practical guidelines for distilling LLMs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) like BERT, RoBERTa, T0, and GPT have set state-of-the-art (SOTA) records on many tasks in natural language processing (NLP). The scaling laws of LLMs clearly push the development of models with billions of parameters. But the growth in model size also makes it unaffordable to deploy LLMs in resource-constrained environments. So knowledge distillation (KD), which is a cost-efficient approach, has attracted attention from researchers who want to distill smaller models that still keep highly competitive performance.

One of the most representative kinds of KD methods is logits-based KD. In logits-based KD the divergence between the distributions of the predicted logits from the teacher and student models is measured and minimized, so that knowledge is transferred. The key to effective logits-based KD is to measure this divergence properly. Existing studies have tried Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, reverse Kullback-Leibler (RKL) divergence, and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence. All of these measures can be seen as variants of the f-divergence measures, and f-divergences are known to be limited when quantifying distributions that lack substantial intersections. Also, as shown in Fig. 1, each measure has its own drawbacks. KL distillation causes a mode-averaging issue, where the student learns an excessively smooth distribution that covers the entire support of the teacher distribution. RKL distillation leads to mode-collapsing, where the student focuses too much on one of the highly probable regions of the teacher distribution and ignores the remaining one. JS distillation causes mode-underestimation, where the student underestimates the probability of rare events because the penalty is insufficient.

There is another challenge when doing sample-wise KD on LLMs. For discriminative tasks, the low-dimensional categorical outputs from the teacher give limited insight into their underlying distributions in the high-dimensional hidden space. An intuitive solution is to use a batch of samples to grasp the distribution differences collectively. But existing divergence measures can only deal with each sample independently, doing logit-by-logit matching, because they are not distance metrics and they cannot locate the paired teacher and student logits of the same sample in the batch for overall distance minimization.

- Sinkhorn Knowledge Distillation (SinKD); logits-based KD for generalizability
- Sinkhorn distance = variant of Wasserstein distance
- Wasserstein: minimum cost to transform one distribution into the other; more sensible cost function; differentiable almost everywhere
- but hard to compute analytically; cost prohibitively high for LLMs
- Sinkhorn: efficient approximation, keeps the benefits, mitigates cost

- sample-wise use feasible but does not exploit perception of structural differences
- Sinkhorn: symmetric metric; derived from optimal transport (OT) -> explicit constraints on matching correctness
- teacher/student batch outputs as sets A and B; minimizing overall distance enforces element-wise matching of same-sample outputs
- -> batch-wise reformulation; capture geometric structures of implicit distributions via low-dimensional observations
- no extra network layer, no task-specific output format changes

6. Experiments
- comparability: BERT on GLUE, consistently beats SOTA KD methods
- validity: ablations and hyper-parameters; advice for practitioners
- generalizability: SuperGLUE with various architectures, encoder-decoder T0 to decoder-only GPT-Neo; prior work only encoder-only BERT

7. Contributions
- SinKD with Sinkhorn distance: addresses KL/RKL/JS limits in extreme scenarios, avoids Wasserstein computation burden
- properties of Sinkhorn distance -> batch-wise OT reformulation
- experiments show superiority over SOTA; practical guidelines for distilling LLMs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) like BERT, RoBERTa, T0, and GPT have set state-of-the-art (SOTA) records on many tasks in natural language processing (NLP). The scaling laws of LLMs clearly push the development of models with billions of parameters. But the growth in model size also makes it unaffordable to deploy LLMs in resource-constrained environments. So knowledge distillation (KD), which is a cost-efficient approach, has attracted attention from researchers who want to distill smaller models that still keep highly competitive performance.

One of the most representative kinds of KD methods is logits-based KD. In logits-based KD the divergence between the distributions of the predicted logits from the teacher and student models is measured and minimized, so that knowledge is transferred. The key to effective logits-based KD is to measure this divergence properly. Existing studies have tried Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, reverse Kullback-Leibler (RKL) divergence, and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence. All of these measures can be seen as variants of the f-divergence measures, and f-divergences are known to be limited when quantifying distributions that lack substantial intersections. Also, as shown in Fig. 1, each measure has its own drawbacks. KL distillation causes a mode-averaging issue, where the student learns an excessively smooth distribution that covers the entire support of the teacher distribution. RKL distillation leads to mode-collapsing, where the student focuses too much on one of the highly probable regions of the teacher distribution and ignores the remaining one. JS distillation causes mode-underestimation, where the student underestimates the probability of rare events because the penalty is insufficient.

There is another challenge when doing sample-wise KD on LLMs. For discriminative tasks, the low-dimensional categorical outputs from the teacher give limited insight into their underlying distributions in the high-dimensional hidden space. An intuitive solution is to use a batch of samples to grasp the distribution differences collectively. But existing divergence measures can only deal with each sample independently, doing logit-by-logit matching, because they are not distance metrics and they cannot locate the paired teacher and student logits of the same sample in the batch for overall distance minimization.

To address these challenges, we propose Sinkhorn Knowledge Distillation, called SinKD, for distillation of LLMs. For generalizability, we tackle logits-based KD in this study, which would benefit a broad range of applications. SinKD uses the Sinkhorn distance, which is a variant of the Wasserstein distance, as the divergence measure. The Wasserstein distance measures the dissimilarity between two distributions by calculating the minimum cost needed to transform one distribution into the other. Compared to traditional divergence measures, it makes more sense as a cost function for distillation. It is also differentiable almost everywhere, which makes optimization easy. But the Wasserstein distance itself is difficult to compute analytically, and the computational cost is prohibitively high for distilling LLMs. So we propose to use the Sinkhorn distance as an efficient approximation, which keeps all the benefits of the Wasserstein distance and also greatly reduces the cost issue.

Applying the Sinkhorn distance directly to sample-wise logits matching is feasible, but it does not take full advantage of how it perceives structural differences in distributions. Luckily, the Sinkhorn distance is a symmetric metric, and since it is derived from optimal transport (OT) it imposes explicit constraints on matching correctness. This means that if we take a batch of logits outputs from the teacher and the student as sets A and B, minimizing the overall Sinkhorn distance between A and B enforces a precise element-wise matching between the two outputs that come from the same sample in the batch. These properties let it work beyond sample-wise distillation, so we propose the batch-wise reformulation. This way we can capture geometric structures of the intricate and implicit distributions even through low-dimensional observations. We do not add any additional network layer or change output formats specific to NLP tasks.

We do extensive experiments in terms of 1) comparability, 2) validity, and 3) generalizability. For comparability, we test SinKD with BERT on the GLUE benchmark and it consistently outperforms the SOTA KD methods. For validity, we give a comprehensive analysis on ablation studies and hyper-parameters, and our findings advise practitioners on how to use SinKD in their own work. For generalizability, we test SinKD on the SuperGLUE benchmark with LLMs of different architectures, from the encoder-decoder T0 to the decoder-only GPT-Neo transformers. SinKD shows robustness across model choices, while previous studies only looked at KD techniques on the encoder-only BERT.

In summary, our contributions are:

- We propose SinKD, a knowledge distillation approach that uses the Sinkhorn distance to measure divergence. It addresses the limitations of KL, RKL, and JS divergences under extreme distribution scenarios, and it also avoids the computation burden of the Wasserstein distance for distillation.

- We look into the properties of the Sinkhorn distance and reformulate SinKD into batch-wise OT, which extends its applicability in NLP tasks.

- Extensive experiments on comparability, validity, and generalizability show that SinKD is better than SOTA methods. We also give practical guidelines for distilling various LLMs for real-world applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) such as BERT [1], RoBERTa [2], T0 [3], and GPT [4,5] have set state-of-the-art (SOTA) records on various tasks in the field of natural language processing (NLP). On one hand, the scaling laws of LLMs clearly stimulate the development of models with billions of parameters. On the other hand, the surge of model size makes it unaffordable for LLMs to be deployed under resource-constrained environments. Consequently, knowledge distillation (KD), a cost-efficient approach, has attracted attention from researchers to distill smaller models which maintain highly competitive performance.

One kind of the most representative KD methods is logits-based KD, where the divergence between the distributions of the predicted logits from teacher and student models is measured and minimized for knowledge transfer. The key to effective logits-based KD is exactly the proper measurement of such divergence. Existing studies have experimented with Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [6], reverse Kullback-Leibler (RKL) divergence [7,8], and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence [9,10,11]. All these measures can be viewed as variants of the f -divergence measures, which are known to be limited in quantification of distributions that lack substantial intersections [12]. Moreover, as illustrated in Fig. 1, each measure has its own drawbacks. KL distillation results in a mode-averaging issue [13,14], causing the student to learn an excessively smooth distribution that encompasses the entire support of the teacher distribution. RKL distillation leads to mode-collapsing [15,9], where the student overly focuses on one of the highly probable regions of the teacher distribution and ignores the remaining one. JS distillation gives rise to mode-underestimation [16,17] where the student underestimates the probability of rare events due to insufficient penalty.

Another challenge of performing sample-wise KD on LLMs is that for discriminative tasks, the low-dimensional categorical outputs from the teacher provide limited insights into their underlying distributions in the high-dimensional hidden space. One intuitive solution is to bring in a batch of samples to collectively grasp the distribution differences. Nevertheless, existing divergence measures can only independently deal with each sample for logit-by-logit matching because they are not distance metrics and cannot locate the paired teacher and student logits of the same sample from the batch for overall distance minimization.

To address these challenges, we propose Sinkhorn Knowledge Distillation, termed as SinKD, for distillation of LLMs. In consideration of generalizability, we tackle logits-based KD in the present study, which would benefit a broad range of applications. Our SinKD employs the Sinkhorn distance [18], a variant of the Wasserstein distance [19,20], as divergence measure. The Wasserstein distance quantifies the dissimilarity between two distributions by calculating the minimum cost required to transform one distribution into the other. Compared with traditional divergence measures, it is more sensible as a cost function for distillation. Furthermore, it is differentiable almost everywhere, enabling easy optimization. Despite these advantages, the Wasserstein distance itself is difficult to be computed analytically, and its computational cost is prohibitively high for distilling LLMs. Under such circumstance, we propose to use Sinkhorn distance as an efficient approximation, which not only retains all the benefits of Wasserstein distance but also greatly mitigates its cost issue.

A straightforward application of Sinkhorn distance on sample-wise logits matching, though feasible, cannot take full advantage of its perception of structural differences in distributions. Luckily, Sinkhorn distance is a symmetric metric and its derivation from the optimal transport (OT) imposes explicit constraints on matching correctness. It means that given a batch of logits outputs from the teacher and the student respectively as sets A and B, the minimization of the overall Sinkhorn distance between A and B enforces a precise element-wise matching between the two outputs coming from the same sample in a batch. Such properties allow it to work beyond sample-wise distillation. As a result, we propose the batch-wise reformulation. In this way, we can capture geometric structures of the intricate and implicit distributions even through low-dimensional observations. We do not introduce additional network layer or modify output formats specific to NLP tasks.

Extensive experiments are conducted in view of 1) comparability, 2) validity, and 3) generalizability. For comparability, we test SinKD with BERT on the GLUE benchmark [21] and it consistently outperforms the SOTA KD methods. For validity, we provide a comprehensive analysis on ablation studies and hyper-parameters, and our findings advise practitioners on how to adopt SinKD in their own work. For generalizability, we test SinKD on the SuperGLUE benchmark [22] with LLMs of various architectures, ranging from the encoder-decoder T0 [3] to the decoder-only GPT-Neo [23] transformers. Our SinKD showcases robustness across model choices while previous studies only investigate KD techniques on the encoder-only BERT.

In summary, our contributions are:

- • We propose SinKD, a knowledge distillation approach that employs the Sinkhorn distance for divergence measurement. It not only addresses limitations of KL, RKL, and JS divergences under extreme distribution scenarios, but also circumvents the computation burden of Wasserstein distance for distillation.

- • We explore the properties of Sinkhorn distance and reformulate SinKD into batch-wise OT, extending its applicability in NLP tasks.

- • Extensive experiments in terms of comparability, validity, and generalizability demonstrate the superiority of SinKD over SOTA methods. We offer practical guidelines of distilling various LLMs for real-world applications.
